title: defer, panic and recover
summary: Cleanup that always runs, arguments frozen early, and the narrow place recover works.

concepts.title: defer
concepts.brief:
A deferred call runs when the **surrounding function** returns — by any route, including a panic. Deferred calls run **last-in, first-out**.

The rule people get wrong: the **arguments are evaluated immediately**, at the `defer` statement. Only the call itself is postponed. So `defer fmt.Println(i)` captures `i` as it is now, not as it will be.

`defer` is what makes cleanup reliable in a language with no destructors and no `finally`: the `Close` sits next to the `Open`, so you can see both at once.

examples.label: Arguments now, call later
examples.note: To capture the final value instead, defer a closure: `defer func() { fmt.Println(i) }()` reads `i` when it runs.

examples.label: LIFO, and why that is the useful order
examples.code:
f, _ := os.Open(path)
defer f.Close()           // runs second

mu.Lock()
defer mu.Unlock()         // runs first

// unwinds in the reverse order it was built up
examples.note: Resources are released in the opposite order to acquisition, which is almost always what correct cleanup requires.

code.label: main.go
code.text:
i := 0
defer fmt.Println("deferred:", i)
i = 42
fmt.Println("direct:", i)

choices: direct: 42 then deferred: 0
direct: 42 then deferred: 42
deferred: 0 then direct: 42
deferred: 42 then direct: 42
items.explain: Arguments are evaluated at the `defer` statement, so `i` was read as 0 and frozen; only the call waits. Wrap it in a closure — `defer func() { fmt.Println(i) }()` — and it reads `i` at run time instead. This is the difference between logging the value you had and the value you ended with.

items.prompt: Three defers registered in this order: A, then B, then C. Put the execution order at return.
steps: C runs first — most recently deferred
then A — the first one registered
and finally the function actually returns to its caller
items.explain: Last in, first out, which mirrors how resources were acquired: unlock before closing the file that the lock protected. It also means a defer registered *after* a failure point does not run if the failure happened first — which is why the `defer f.Close()` goes immediately after the error check on `Open`, never before it.

items.prompt: You `defer f.Close()` inside a loop over 10,000 files, in one long function.
choices: All 10,000 stay open until the function returns — likely too many open files
Each closes at the end of its loop iteration
Only the last one is deferred; earlier defers are replaced
It does not compile; defer is not allowed in a loop
items.explain: `defer` is scoped to the **function**, not the block, so they pile up and you hit the file-descriptor limit with `too many open files`. The fix is to give each iteration its own function — move the body into a closure called inside the loop, or a named helper — so its defers run per iteration.

items.prompt: You write to a file and use `defer f.Close()`, ignoring its error. What can that hide?
choices: A failed flush — buffered writes can fail at Close, losing the tail of the data
Nothing; Close on a file never fails
Only a double-close, which is harmless
A missing Sync, which Close never performs
items.explain: For anything buffered, `Close` is where the last write is flushed and therefore where it can fail — so discarding that error can silently truncate a file you just wrote. For reads, ignoring it is fine. For writes, capture it in a named return: `defer func() { err = errors.Join(err, f.Close()) }()`.

items.prompt: A function has deferred cleanup, and somewhere inside it calls `os.Exit(1)`.
choices: No defers run — os.Exit terminates immediately
Defers in the current function run, but not in its callers
All pending defers run, then the process exits
It panics first, so defers run during the unwind
items.explain: `os.Exit` stops the process on the spot: no defers, no flushes, no cleanup. `log.Fatal` calls it, which is why a `log.Fatal` deep inside a request handler skips every `Close` and `Unlock` on the stack. Keep exits in `main`, and return errors everywhere else.

concepts.title: defer and named return values
concepts.brief:
A deferred closure can **change what the function returns**, but only if the return values are **named**.

`return x` with named results is really two steps: assign `x` to the result variable, then run the defers, then return whatever the result variable now holds. A defer that assigns to it wins.

This is the mechanism behind the two legitimate uses of named returns: turning a recovered panic into an error, and joining a `Close` error onto the one you were already returning. Outside those, named returns mostly hurt readability.

examples.label: Rewriting the error on the way out
examples.note: Every error path gets the same context without repeating the wrap at each `return`.

examples.label: Not naming them means you cannot
examples.note: With unnamed results the returned value is copied before defers run, so there is nothing left to modify.

items.prompt: `func f() (err error)` returns nil, and a deferred closure sets `err = errors.New("boom")`. What does the caller see?
choices: The boom error — the defer assigned to the named result before it was returned
nil — the return value was already decided
The boom error only if the function panicked
A compile error about assigning to a return value
items.explain: `return nil` sets the result variable `err` to nil, *then* defers run and overwrite it, *then* the function returns. That ordering is the whole feature, and it is also why a stray assignment in a defer can change a function's result in a way that is easy to miss when reading.

items.prompt: Same thing but the signature is `func f() error` with a local `var err error`.
choices: The caller sees nil — the defer assigns a local that is no longer the result
The caller sees the boom error, the same as with a named result
It does not compile
The behavior is undefined and varies by Go version
items.explain: Without a name there is no result variable to assign to: the value is copied out at `return`, and the defer just modifies a local nobody reads again. If you want a defer to influence the result, the result must be named — there is no other way.

items.prompt: Put `return parse(f)` in a function with named results in order.
steps: Its values are assigned to the named result variables
Deferred calls run, and may change those variables
The function returns whatever the result variables now hold
items.explain: Three steps, not one — and the defers sit in the middle. Knowing this ordering is what makes the recover-to-error pattern obvious rather than magic: the deferred function runs after the result has been set but before the caller can see it.

items.prompt: Why does `defer func() { err = errors.Join(err, f.Close()) }()` need a named `err`?
choices: It has to modify the value being returned, which only a named result allows
errors.Join requires its arguments to be addressable
Because Close must run before the return value is computed
It does not; any local err works
items.explain: The whole point is to change what the caller receives — so a write to a local is useless. This pattern is how you stop discarding a `Close` error on a file you wrote, without an `if` at every return. `errors.Join` handles the case where both are non-nil.

concepts.title: panic and recover
concepts.brief:
`panic` stops the current function, runs its deferred calls, and does the same up the stack. If nothing stops it, the program prints the panic and the goroutine's stack, then exits.

`recover` stops that unwinding, but only under narrow conditions:

- It must be called **inside a deferred function** — directly, not nested one level deeper.
- It only catches panics in the **same goroutine**.
- It returns `nil` when there is no panic, which is how you tell.

A **fatal error** — concurrent map writes, out of memory, a deadlock — is not a panic and `recover` cannot touch it.

examples.label: The only shape that works
examples.note: Deferred closure, `recover()` called directly inside it, named return so the panic becomes an error the caller can handle.

examples.label: Each goroutine is on its own
examples.note: A goroutine that can panic needs its own deferred recover, inside itself. There is no parent to catch it.

items.prompt: Where must `recover()` be called to actually stop a panic?
choices: Directly inside a deferred function in the panicking goroutine
Anywhere in the function that panicked
In the caller of the function that panicked
Inside any deferred function, in any goroutine
items.explain: Directly inside a deferred function, same goroutine. Call it in a helper that the deferred function calls and it returns nil — the panic carries on. That restriction is why you see the slightly awkward `defer func() { if r := recover(); ... }()` everywhere instead of a tidy `defer handlePanic()`.

items.prompt: `main` has a deferred recover. A goroutine it started panics.
choices: The process dies — recover only works in the goroutine that panicked
main's recover catches it and the program continues
The panic is re-raised in main when it next blocks
The goroutine dies quietly and the rest keeps running
items.explain: Panics do not cross goroutines, and there is no parent-child relationship to propagate along. Any goroutine doing work that could panic needs its own deferred recover — which is exactly what `net/http` does on the goroutines it starts, and why a panicking handler does not take the server down.

choices: A nil map write
An index out of range
Concurrent map writes
A deadlock of all goroutines
items.explain: The first two are panics and are recoverable. The last two are **fatal errors** — the runtime prints `fatal error:` rather than `panic:` and exits without running deferred functions, deliberately, because the program's state is no longer trustworthy. Reading that first word of the crash tells you whether any recover could ever have helped.

items.prompt: You recover, inspect the value, and decide it is not yours to handle. What should you do?
choices: `panic(r)` again — re-panicking resumes the unwinding
Return the value as an error; the panic is already stopped
Call runtime.Goexit() to end the goroutine cleanly
Nothing — a recovered panic resumes automatically if unhandled
items.explain: `panic(r)` restarts the unwind from here. The stack trace then shows the re-panic point rather than the original, which is why a recover that might re-panic should log the original stack with `debug.PrintStack()` before deciding. Recovering only to swallow something you did not understand is how bugs become invisible.

items.prompt: Complete the guard that detects whether a panic is in progress: `if r := ______; r != nil {`
items.explain: `recover()`. It returns the value passed to `panic`, or nil if there is no panic — so the nil check *is* the detection. Calling it when nothing panicked is harmless and returns nil, which is why the idiom is safe to leave in place permanently.
